note: Municipality. No recogniser has Caibiran in its vocabulary, so it snaps to the nearest common word - kaibigan, Tagalog for friend. Observed on a real handset: "Mayda sunog didi ha Caibiran" -> "mayda sunog didiha kaibigan kaibigan".
Word-boundary merge. The phonemes were right; the recogniser just did not split them. `didi` (Waray: here) and `ha` (at) are both in local_language_terms.csv individually.
Two. The o/u vowel swap, on a numeral. Observed clip 1: "duha ka tawo an naipit" -> "doha kataw anaipit". Recovers injured_count and people_involved, which are otherwise simply absent.
Inside. "sa sulod" is the phrase TRAPPED_AFFIRM matches on, so without this a report saying someone is inside a burning house yields no entrapment signal at all. Observed clip 1.

Word-boundary merge of "an nasamdan". The injury still matched, because nasamdan is findable inside the merged token; the COUNT did not, because _count() needs the numeral and the noun as separate words. Observed clip 3.

Fire, with an inserted n. No sound rule reaches an added letter -- phonetic.key('sunong') != key('sunog') -- so this needs an exact row. Fire confidence 0.96 -> 1.00. Observed on the first recorded clip.

"tulo ka tawo" welded into one token. Added as an EXACT row, which is different in kind from un-gluing algorithmically: a person confirmed this specific string against the recording. The general case stays a warning -- see _glued_number_words. Observed clip 3.

Code-switch collapse. The resident said `disgrasya` (accident); the recogniser reached for English and produced `nerescrash`. No sound rule connects them -- phonetic.key('nerescrash')='niriskrash' vs key('disgrasya')='disgrasia' -- so this needs an exact row. `disgrasya` is emergency vocabulary; without it the report carries no incident word at all. Observed INC-C38001, confirmed by the reporter.

Word-boundary merge: the classifier `ka` welded onto `motor`. Splitting it restores the `<numeral> ka <noun>` shape predict._count() needs, without which a vehicle count cannot be read. Observed INC-C38001, confirmed by the reporter.

Epenthetic h plus a boundary merge. `banggaay` IS in emergency_terms.csv, but the nag- prefix and the inserted h both change the phonetic key (nagbangahai vs bangai), so the sound layer cannot reach a word the system already knows. Corrected to two tokens so `banggaay` matches the vocabulary directly. Observed INC-C38001, confirmed by the reporter.

Two. The numeral was replaced wholesale by a non-word -- `yado` is not Waray, Cebuano, Tagalog or English. Recovers vehicles_involved=2, which the reporter stated and the transcript destroyed. RISK: this is a count, and a wrong count is worse than a missing one. It is defensible only because `yado` is a non-word in every language Ziren reads, so it cannot displace a real one. Revisit if it ever appears in another context. Observed INC-C38001, confirmed by the reporter.

Second recorded mangling of `disgrasya`, from the SAME sentence that produced `nerescrash` on an earlier take. Neither the sound layer (diskursiadu vs disgrasia) nor the fuzzy pass (ratio 70, threshold 78) reaches it. Observed INC-35572A, confirmed by the reporter.

Second recorded mangling of `nag banggaay`, after `nagbanggahay` on an earlier take of the same sentence. A rule collapsing ngk->ng would catch it and would also merge `bangka` (boat) with `bangga` (collision) -- unacceptable in a coastal municipality, so this stays an exact row. Observed INC-35572A, confirmed by the reporter.

Fifth recorded mangling of `disgrasya`, after nerescrash, discursyado and two takes where the word did not come back at all. The recogniser breaks the `sgr` cluster with an epenthetic vowel -- dis-gras-ya heard as dis-kur-as-yan -- which is an inserted syllable, not a phoneme swap, so no sound rule reaches it. Tested: a g/k merge is safe but does not unify the forms, and a consonant-skeleton match unifies nothing while colliding baha/bahay and balay/bali, which is the failure that disabled the fuzzy pass. Observed INC (take 5), confirmed by the reporter.

Sixth mangling of `disgrasya`, and the second time this exact form came back -- takes 6 and 8 of the same sentence -- so it is the recogniser's settled output for the word, not noise. Added despite `disgrasya` driving no signal and no severity: it lands where the incident word belongs and misleads anyone reading the report, which is the comprehension requirement the dashboard panel exists to serve. Safe because `discretion` occurs in 0 of the 1829 reports in classification_dataset.csv, so it cannot displace legitimate English. Confirmed by the reporter.
